chunks: And Ahmad ibn 'Abdun informed me, from 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn al-Zubayr, from 'Ali ibn al-Hasan, from 'Ali ibn Asbat, from Hakam ibn Miskin, from Abu al-Mustahall, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, from Abu 'Abd Allah (AS):
He said: «Indeed, Moses (AS) said: 'O Lord, there come upon me states in which I am too shy to mention You.' He [God] said: 'O Moses, My remembrance in every state is good.'»
As for the dislike (karahah) of speech [during such states], that has indeed been narrated.

key_terms.أَسْتَحْيِي: I am too shy, I feel embarrassed — religious modesty before God's majesty
key_terms.حَالَاتٌ: states, conditions — here: states of ritual impurity (hadath) during which one relieves oneself
key_terms.ذِكْرِي: My remembrance — God's own word for dhikr; the mention or invocation of the Divine name
key_terms.كَرَاهِيَةُ: legal discouragedness, makruh — an act not forbidden but disapproved of in Islamic jurisprudence

ai.seo_question: Is dhikr (remembrance of God) permissible during states of ritual impurity according to Shia hadith from Tahdhib al-Ahkam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) narrates that the Prophet Moses (AS) confessed to his Lord that certain states — understood in this jurisprudential chapter on acts requiring purification as states of ritual impurity — made him too shy to utter God's name. God's response was unequivocal: 'O Moses, My remembrance in every state is good.' Shaykh al-Tusi appends an editorial note clarifying that while dhikr is always permitted, the makruh (discouraged) status of unnecessary speech during such states has also been separately transmitted.
